pr.title: coverage: Remove incorrect assertions from counter allocation
pr.description:
These assertions detect situations where a BCB node (in the coverage graph) would have both a physical counter and one or more in-edge counters/expressions.

For most BCBs that situation would indicate an implementation bug. However, it's perfectly fine in the case of a BCB having an edge that loops back to itself.

Given the complexity and risk involved in fixing the assertions, and the fact that nothing relies on them actually being true, this patch just removes them instead.

Fixes #122738.

analysis.originalLogic: In `compiler/rustc_mir_transform/src/coverage/counters.rs`, `CoverageCounters` tracked BCBs that had incoming edge counters in `bcb_has_incoming_edge_counters: BitSet<BasicCoverageBlock>`. `set_bcb_counter` asserted `counter_kind.is_expression() || !self.bcb_has_incoming_edge_counters.contains(bcb)` with the message "attempt to add a `Counter` to a BCB target with existing incoming edge counters". `set_bcb_edge_counter` similarly checked whether the target BCB already had a non-expression node counter and called `bug!` if so, then inserted `to_bcb` into the BitSet. These encoded the assumption that a BCB node must not simultaneously receive a physical counter and an incoming edge counter (expressions were allowed).
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historical implementation treated "a BCB node never has both a physical counter and an incoming edge counter/expression" as a hard invariant and aborted compilation with an ICE when the condition occurred. That transformation is incorrect for a BCB with a self-loop edge (`from_bcb == to_bcb`): such a node can legitimately have both its own physical counter and an edge counter on its in-edge. The fix removes the assertions and the tracking BitSet rather than rejecting or changing the valid counter allocation.
analysis.inputDomain: MIR coverage graph BasicCoverageBlocks produced while compiling Rust functions with `-Cinstrument-coverage`, especially functions containing tight self-loops or diverging branches. The regression input uses `let true = cond else { loop {} };` (let-else with a loop in the else branch), with variants that also have `loop {}` on the success path and an `if cond { loop {} } else { loop {} }` variant.
analysis.summary: Bug-fix PR for rust-lang/rust#122738: the InstrumentCoverage counter-allocation code contained over-strict assertions claiming a BCB node cannot have both a physical counter and one or more incoming edge counters/expressions. Such a combination is valid when a BCB has an edge looping back to itself, so the assertions caused an ICE. The patch removes the assertions and their supporting BitSet instead of trying to repair them.
analysis.trigger: Counter allocation reaches a BasicCoverageBlock that has an edge looping back to itself, so the same BCB is both the edge target with an incoming edge counter and the node receiving a physical counter. The pre-fix assertions then panic; for example, the issue reports `attempt to add a `Counter` to a BCB target with existing incoming edge counters`.
preconditions: The function's coverage graph contains a BCB with a self-loop edge (the node is also the source of its in-edge).
Counter allocation assigns both an edge counter to that in-edge and a physical counter to the same BCB.

The input shape can arise from let-else with a diverging else branch such as `let true = cond else { loop {} };`, optionally with another `loop {}` on the success path or an if/else where both arms diverge.
pitfalls: Do not assume a BCB with incoming edge counters can never also need its own physical counter; self-loops make that combination legal.
The assertion's invariant is not required for correctness: the PR states that "nothing relies on them actually being true", so removing them is safe and preferable to a risky allocation rewrite.

Do not conflate this with arbitrary BCB loops; the problematic case is specifically an edge whose source and target BCB are the same (a tight self-loop), not merely any loop back-edge between distinct BCBs.
The regression test was initially added with `//@ ignore-test` and then un-ignored in the same PR, so the final test is expected to run and check coverage output rather than being skipped.
analysis.testStrategy: Add a focused `tests/coverage/let_else_loop.rs` regression test plus `.coverage` and `.cov-map` expectations. Compile with coverage instrumentation and check that counter allocation completes without an ICE. Include the minimal let-else self-loop case `fn loopy(cond: bool) { let true = cond else { loop {} }; }`, a variant with `loop {}` also on the success path, and an `if`/`else` variant with `loop {}` in both arms to guard against regressions. Verify the expected coverage map shows physical counters on the loop-containing function (the `.cov-map` expects `Code(Counter(0))` and `Code(Counter(1))` for `loopy`). Use `#[coverage(off)]` on `main` so only the intended functions are instrumented.
evidence: These assertions detect situations where a BCB node (in the coverage graph) would have both a physical counter and one or more in-edge counters/expressions.
For most BCBs that situation would indicate an implementation bug. However, it's perfectly fine in the case of a BCB having an edge that loops back to itself.
Given the complexity and risk involved in fixing the assertions, and the fact that nothing relies on them actually being true, this patch just removes them instead.
